opus-5.5.text:
I think there are real opportunities, but you have to be honest about where they are and where they aren't.

The foundation model companies are improving very quickly, and every time a new model comes out, a lot of the "agent" products built on top of the previous model simply get absorbed. If your entire value is a clever prompt or a thin workflow wrapper around a general capability, like generic browsing or generic coding, then you're standing exactly where the model labs are heading, and they will eventually do it better and cheaper. So I would not recommend building in the direct path of the base model's general capability curve.

Where I do see opportunity is in three places.

First, the environment. An agent is not just a model. It's a model interacting with an environment: tools, data, permissions, feedback signals. In many verticals, the hard part isn't reasoning. It's that the environment is messy, private, and long-tailed. Enterprise systems, specific industry software, internal knowledge, workflows that never show up on the public internet. If a startup really understands one such environment deeply and builds the infrastructure for an agent to act reliably inside it, that's something a general model company won't prioritize for a long time.

Second, data and feedback loops. From a reinforcement learning perspective, what really makes an agent better is the reward signal, knowing what "good" looks like in a specific task and collecting trajectories of success and failure. A startup that owns real user interactions in a domain accumulates data the labs don't have. And now that open-source models are quite strong, you don't need to pretrain your own foundation model. You can do post-training, RL fine-tuning on your own tasks, and get a specialized model that beats a general model in your niche, at much lower cost.

Third, product and human-agent interaction. Even if the model is capable, figuring out how humans delegate, supervise, correct, and trust an agent is a product problem, not a model problem. Many people underestimate this. A lot of the value comes from designing the right interaction loop.

So my view is: don't compete with the foundation model on intelligence itself. Treat the model as a rapidly improving component, and build things that become more valuable as the model gets stronger, not less. If a better base model makes your product better, you're in a good position. If a better base model makes your product unnecessary, that's a warning sign.

And one more point: speed matters a lot. The window is open now, while capabilities are good enough to be useful but not yet packaged end-to-end by the big players. Startups that move fast, find a real use case, and start the data flywheel early can build a moat that's hard to replicate later.

r002.rationale: It discusses vertical environments and agent infrastructure, but does not characterize serving those verticals as fundamentally a B2B service business.

r003.rationale: It makes no claim about China or why China has fewer agent startups.

r004.rationale: It says a startup with real user interactions in a domain can accumulate data the labs lack and use it to outperform a general model in its niche, expressing a potential data advantage over foundation model companies such as OpenAI.

r005.rationale: It describes a current window before big players package capabilities end to end, but does not frame the opportunity as preceding OpenAI's application of large-scale reinforcement learning to the domain.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the opportunity is real, but you have to be honest about where it sits.

If you don't have your own foundation model, you don't own the intelligence. What you can own is the environment: the data, the tools, the feedback loop, the user. So the question for a startup isn't "can we build a smarter agent than the labs," because you can't, the base model decides most of that. The question is "can we put the model in a position where it compounds in a way the lab can't replicate."

Concretely, that means a few things. First, pick a domain where the task has a clear notion of success, so you can collect signal. Agents are RL systems in disguise, whether you train the weights or not. If you can tell when the agent did well and when it didn't, you can improve prompts, retrieval, tool design, verification, all of that, and that loop is your moat. Second, go deep into a workflow where integration is the hard part. Coding agents are the obvious example, but there are many less glamorous ones: finance back office, legal review, operations. Those domains are messy and the labs won't want to understand them. Third, design for model churn. The model you build on today will be replaced in six months. If your product gets better when the base model gets better, you're in a good place. If a better model makes your product unnecessary, you were only ever a wrapper.

I'd also say the window is wider than people think, because the labs are constrained. They have a handful of priorities, they're mostly building horizontal products, and their incentive is to make the model good, not to make your vertical work. But the window isn't forever. As models get more agentic out of the box, a lot of what startups do today in orchestration, planning, memory, that moves into the model. So you have to keep moving up: from making the agent work at all, to making it work in your customer's specific reality, to owning the data and relationships that come from that.

The last thing I'd say, from my own experience doing RL, is that even without a foundation model, you can still train. Fine-tuning small models for sub-tasks, training reward models, building evaluation environments: these are all accessible to a small team now. You don't need to pretrain to have a technical edge. You need to have an environment nobody else has.

r002.rationale: It discusses vertical workflows and integration, but does not characterize serving them as fundamentally a B2B service business.

r003.rationale: It does not mention China or attribute fewer agent startups there to difficulty building vertical B2B services.

r004.rationale: It says a startup can own data and a domain-specific environment that labs cannot replicate, describing these as a moat and potential technical edge.

r005.rationale: It describes a window before agent capabilities move into models, but does not frame the opportunity as ending when OpenAI applies large-scale reinforcement learning to the startup’s domain.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a lot of opportunity. You don’t necessarily need to train your own foundation model to build a useful agent. The model gives you a general capability, but turning that capability into something that reliably solves a customer’s problem requires a lot of additional work.

For a startup, the key is to understand a particular workflow deeply. What information does the agent need? Which tools should it use? When should it ask a human for help? And how do you measure whether it actually completed the task? Those are product and engineering problems, and owning the foundation model doesn’t automatically solve them.

Of course, there’s a risk if your product is just a thin layer around something the next model release can do directly. I would focus on a specific customer problem, build the integrations, and create a feedback loop that helps you improve from real usage. Then better foundation models become an advantage: you can use them to deliver a better product.

r001.rationale: The response discusses workflow-specific product work, but does not say that near-universal foundation-model coverage would still leave a large absolute number of uncovered cases.

r002.rationale: It describes building agents for particular workflows, but does not characterize serving underserved verticals as fundamentally a B2B service business.

r003.rationale: The response makes no claim about China or why it has fewer agent startups.

r004.rationale: It mentions feedback from real usage, but does not identify accumulating better vertical-specific data as an advantage over OpenAI.

r005.rationale: It mentions the risk of model releases subsuming a thin product layer, but does not frame the opportunity as a window before OpenAI applies large-scale reinforcement learning to a domain.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a lot of room for startups. You don’t necessarily need to own the foundation model to build a valuable agent. The model gives you a general capability, but there’s still a lot of work involved in turning that capability into something that reliably solves a customer’s problem.

For example, an agent needs access to the right information and tools. It needs to understand the workflow, know when to ask for help, and let the user verify what it has done. A startup can create a lot of value by getting those details right in a particular domain.

The challenge is that foundation models keep improving. If your product only compensates for something today’s model cannot do, that advantage might disappear with the next release. So I would focus on a customer problem where better models make your product more useful, and where your understanding of the workflow, your integrations, and the feedback you get from users keep accumulating.

In that sense, not having your own model can actually give you flexibility. You can use whichever model works best for the task. The important question is whether you can deliver a useful outcome consistently enough that people want to rely on it.
